*Among the neurological disease known as "amnesic syndrome," which is a broader definition of memory loss, my symptoms point to a particular form called lacunar amnesia apparently.*
*Memory is generally subdivided into two large categories, declarative memory and procedural memory. Defined simply, the former can be expressed through words, while the latter cannot.*
*The memory which "cannot be expressed through words" mainly consists of motor skills and memorization of how to do various things.*
*Basically memory that details how to use objects and move your body accordingly, like when playing an instrument or doing some sport.*
*The memory that I've lost is one you can express through words, declarative memory. The general term for all forms of impairment with regards to the declarative memory is amnesia.*
*Amnesia is also subdivided into two forms, total amnesia and lacunar amnesia.*
*The former is when you forget all memories within a specific time frame, while the latter is when you only forget a certain piece of your memories for a certain time frame.*
*Accordingly, one can deduce that I am suffering from lacunar amnesia.*
*There are many things that can result in lacunar amnesia, it seems.*
*They range from psychological causes, such as stress, to physical trauma like injuries, as well as diseases or drug usage.*
*In my particular case... I can't judge which applies.*
*Anyhow, the most important thing is that the method of treatment for lacunar amnesia is awfully simple.*
*In the majority of cases, when it comes to lacunar amnesia, the lost memories normally come back on their own after a certain amount of time passes, which can be as little as a few days, to as long as one or two months.*
*Medical treatment in the form of hypnotherapy and electroshock therapy is an option as well it seems, but these books seem to advise against going with those options.*
*Even if you ignore it entirely, the brain cures memory loss on its own.*

*When it comes to what situations cause people to hallucinate, there are multiple such possibilities.*

*In Psychology, there is a term, "self-defense mechanism."*
*When a person receives stimuli that may prove mentally damaging, the brain subconsciously attempts to find a way that upholds one's well-being, and chooses certain methods to meet that end.*
*That contrivance of our mind is generally what is referred to as a "self-defense mechanism."*
*Take, for instance, when you can't get a good score on an exam despite putting in hours of studying. You then naturally try to justify the outcome through any way possible. That is what we refer to as "rationalization."*
*Besides that, we can also look at a situation like when your school defeats another school in a sports match and you then boast about it as if you were the one who was down there playing the game. That is what we call "identification."*
*Yet another example is the way in which people often tease the person they have a crush on. That is referred to as "reaction formation."*
